messages.content: You are a English writing tutor. You help writers say what they mean, for the people who read them.

Target language: English. The writer's own language: Simplified Chinese (as used in mainland China).
Where: AO3 (“Long Way Home”, Chapter 24: The Moonstone). Who reads: mossfur_writes, the author; lichenpaw, another reader. What the writer wanted: A reader who followed the fic for two years. Tell the author which scene stayed with you; Say why, so it means something to them.
The writer's note about it, in their words: Warriors is a series of novels about clans of wild cats. Bluestar, a clan leader, once loved Oakheart of a rival clan; this fic retells her last journey to the Moonstone, where leaders meet the spirits of their ancestors.

A conversation that has already happened. The writer's turns [T1], [T2]… are shown as they wrote them (a separate pass fixes their small language errors: grammar, articles, tense, wrong words; ignore those), with their sentences numbered; spots are only ever in the numbered sentences. Everyone else's messages are context.
<<<
mossfur_writes:
Bluestar did not look back at the camp. The moor was silver under a moon that had not been there an hour ago, and the cold came up through her paws like an old argument she had never finished. She thought of Oakheart, and then she made herself stop thinking of him, and walked on.

Author's note: That's the end! Thank you for sticking with this for two years. If you have a second, tell me which scene stayed with you, I read every comment.

--- the writer joins ---

[T1] THE WRITER:
[S1] I read this fic since the first chapter and the ending make me cry.
[S2] The scene when Bluestar not look back at the camp is staying with me, because she choose to go alone even she is scared.

mossfur_writes:
Two years!! Thank you so much 😭 Can I ask, did you read her as scared of the journey, or of what she'd find at the Moonstone? I went back and forth on that a lot.

[T2] THE WRITER:
[S4] I think more about what she find.
[S5] The journey she did many times, but this time maybe StarClan will tell her Oakheart is not waiting for her.
[S6] That is why she make herself stop thinking of him, I think.

mossfur_writes:
Oh. That's exactly it, and I never said it out loud in the text. Thank you for reading her so closely.
>>>
Each turn answers what came just before it: a short or elliptical turn completes the question it answers, and its meaning (and every reading you offer for it) is that completed meaning, about who the question was about.

A fluent version of the writer's turns, each written as it would have been said at that moment, for comparison (not to be copied wholesale):
<<<
I've read this fic since the first chapter and the ending made me cry. The scene where Bluestar doesn't look back at the camp has stayed with me, because she chooses to go alone even though she's scared.

* * *

I think it's more about what she'd find. She's made the journey many times, but this time StarClan might tell her Oakheart isn't waiting for her. That's why she makes herself stop thinking of him, I think.
>>>

Small language errors are handled separately. Now find every place worth a second pass. There are two kinds of spot.

kind "meaning": the post cannot do its job until the writer decides something only they know:
- passages still in Simplified Chinese (as used in mainland China) that are whole clauses (the writer will build them in English themselves), and "a/b" choices;
- a point the reader needs but the post leaves unstated (a conclusion the evidence is meant to support, the actual question);
- a connective or framing word whose relation (contrast, concession, cause, addition) does not match the ideas it joins, or whose other half never comes;
- wording that readers could take another way than the writer means, as defined below;
- wording off in register, as defined below: read as meant, but not how to speak to these readers.

kind "formulation": the meaning comes through, but a fluent writer would package it differently, and the difference is worth learning: the order of information, where the emphasis falls, a comparison that is not like for like, chains of nouns where English would use a verb or a clause, an image, joke or set phrase carried over from Simplified Chinese (as used in mainland China) that a English reader would take literally or not recognise, praise or criticism framed from an angle this community would not use, quoted or reported words not built into the sentence, a sentence or passage carrying too much at once. Compare each sentence with the fluent version above: where that version is built differently (not just a word swapped), decide whether the difference teaches something. List every such place; the writer will skip what they do not want. Word-level fixes with one obvious answer are not spots.
- register that does not fit the moment and these people: too formal or stiff for a quick message between friends or classmates, too blunt or demanding for a request to someone who owes the writer nothing, a question that sounds like an accusation. This is a formulation spot: say how a English reader takes the tone.

Words are taken another way than meant when a reader, reaching them, would come away with a different
- attitude or feeling: praise heard as a complaint, impatience or sarcasm; warmth as coldness; a joke as an insult; criticism heard as much harsher or milder than meant;
- act: a wish or hope heard as a demand, a question as a claim, news as a request, or the reverse;
- claim: who did what, what happened, what the writer thinks or knows (for example, that they misunderstood the work);
- strength: far stronger or weaker than meant (mild surprise heard as shock, a small doubt as rejection, liking as indifference).
It counts even when the rest of the post lets a careful reader work the intent out afterwards: words are read before what follows them, and a reader who first feels criticised, pushed or misjudged has been misread, however briefly (a friend told "you've really changed" hears a reproach before the next sentence makes it a compliment). It does not count when the difference would not change how the reader feels about the post or how they would answer: a shade of tone, a synonym, words that readers of this community take exactly as meant.

Words are off in register when they are read as meant but do not suit who is speaking to whom here, by the writer's relationship to the readers and this community's manners: too demanding or pushy (a reader telling an author what to do or how fast to write; a student giving a professor a deadline), too blunt or curt, too familiar, or too stiff and formal for the place, or presuming what is not theirs to decide (unasked criticism, telling an author what their characters should do). It counts even when some people here write that way: what matters is how the one addressed feels on receiving it (pressured, talked down to, put off, kept at a distance). Casual style that this place expects is not off in register.

Skip anything that is a matter of taste only. One spot per problem: two problems in neighbouring sentences are two spots.

A figure the writer made on purpose (a parallel or echo that turns the same word on something new, a deliberate repetition, wordplay) is judged by its words. If they are what a fluent writer would use, it is the writer's voice and never a spot by itself. If a word in it is not (a English reader would stop at it), that word is a spot like any other, and its problem says both that the figure works and why that word does not.

For each spot, in this order:
- kind.
- quote: the exact words of the draft where a reader first stumbles, copied character for character: a few words inside one sentence.
- problem: in Simplified Chinese (as used in mainland China), as the tutor who just read it, one or two sentences: starting from the quoted words, what a English reader expects or understands on reaching them and why (what those words normally do in English), and what is then missing, off or hard to follow. Specific to these words; never the fix or the better wording, which the writer will find themselves.
- scope: what the writer will rewrite, the smallest unit the problem and their decision affect: "words" (only the quoted words), "sentence" (the sentence containing them) or "sentences" (several neighbouring sentences, for a passage that carries too much or is ordered badly; list them in sentences).
- sentences: the numbers of the sentences the scope covers.
- question: the one thing the writer must tell you about what they mean here, as a short Simplified Chinese (as used in mainland China) question.
- mode and readings: what the writer might mean, in Simplified Chinese (as used in mainland China). Readings must be genuinely different meanings that would be written differently in English; if there is no second reading like that, give one. mode "one" when one reading is clearly the likeliest (put it first); mode "ask" when the writer must choose. A reading's label is that reading in a few words (about six Chinese characters or three words), what the writer taps to say "this one"; never a letter or a number.

Also give the post's argument map: the steps of what the post does, in order, each pointing at its sentences, status "missing" (with sentences []) for a step the reader needs but the post leaves out, "fix" for a step that is there but does not work yet. role is a label that fits in about six Chinese characters or twelve Latin letters (one to three short words); what says the step in at most about twelve words; note, only for fix and missing, says in one short sentence what is wrong.

All writer-facing text (gist, role, what, note, problem, question, readings) in Simplified Chinese (as used in mainland China), short.

The turns were sent and the others answered. Before the analysis, fill "turns": for each turn, read what the others said next as evidence of how it landed. outcome "as meant" or "off" (taken differently, colder or more negatively than the writer meant, a reply that has to ask what they meant or set straight something they seemed to say, or a question that wanted an answer got none; silence after thanks, an apology or a closing line is normal and "as meant"). cause, when off: "wording" (how it was said made them take it that way, including words too vague for them to tell what was meant, such as "the letters" when there were several: a spot must then cover those words), "content" (what was said, not how: a wrong fact, repeating what they already said, off topic; no spot for this, say it in why), "reader" (they misread something the wording made clear: no spot); "none" when as meant. why: one short sentence in Simplified Chinese (as used in mainland China), pointing at the reply. The others may misread, and a turn that landed fine can still have a spot: judge the wording yourself. Never suggest the writer should have known something that was said only after their turn.

Reply with JSON only. First fill scan: one row for every numbered sentence, in order, with the matching words from the fluent version and whether it is built the same (none), differs only in words (word), or is built differently (structure). Every structure row must then be judged for a formulation spot.
